🧠 Project: Impact of Short-Term Rentals on the Housing Market¶

This notebook is part of Phase 2 of the project for the course Information Integration and Analytic Processing.

📌 Objectives:

  • Integrate data from multiple sources.
  • Analyze the relationship between short-term rental density, population, and rental prices.
  • Implement data cleaning, schema integration, and identity resolution techniques.

1.📦 Data Overview¶

1.1 Data Sources¶

In this section, we import the different datasets required to analyze the impact of short-term rentals on urban areas in Portugal. Each dataset comes from a distinct source and provides a specific perspective on urban characteristics, such as population density, rental supply, housing prices, and administrative divisions.

The datasets imported are as follows:

  • portugal_listings.csv: Contains information about properties available for purchase across the country, including fields like Price, District, City, and Town.
    Source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/luvathoms/portugal-real-estate-2024

  • rendasm2.json: Provides average rental prices per square meter for different regions in 2023.
    Source: https://www.ine.pt/bddXplorer/htdocs/minfo.jsp?var_cd=0012600&lingua=PT

  • densidadePopulacional.json: Indicates population density (inhabitants/km²) by municipality for 2023.
    Source: https://www.ine.pt/bddXplorer/htdocs/minfo.jsp?var_cd=0008337&lingua=PT

  • densidadealojamentosm2.json: Presents the density of short-term rental units (units/km²) at the parish level, for 2021.
    Source: https://www.ine.pt/bddXplorer/htdocs/minfo.jsp?var_cd=0012514&lingua=PT

  • Areas_Freg_Conc_Dist_Pais_CAOP2019.xls: The CAOP (Carta Administrativa Oficial de Portugal) file defines the country’s administrative structure, including districts, municipalities, and parishes. It is used as a reference to unify geographic codes (DICO, geocod, etc.).
    Source: https://www.dgterritorio.gov.pt/cartografia/cartografia-tematica/caop

⚠️ Each file was loaded based on its internal structure (.csv, .json, .xls) and only the relevant content was extracted for further cleaning and integration.

Note:
For spatial visualizations, regional boundary data from CAOP 2021 was used (public domain).
Files were retrieved from nmota/caop_GeoJSON and merged into a single GeoJSON file for plotting purposes.

1.2 Data Import¶

In [52]:
import pandas as pd

# Load dataset with property listings available for sale
property_listings = pd.read_csv(r'dados\portugal_listings.csv')

# Load dataset with average rental prices per square meter for 2023
rental_prices_raw = pd.read_json(r'dados\rendasm2.json')
rental_prices = pd.DataFrame(rental_prices_raw['Dados'][0]['2023'])

# Load dataset with population density (inhabitants/km²) by municipality for 2023
population_density_raw = pd.read_json(r'dados\densidadePopulacional.json')
population_density = pd.DataFrame(population_density_raw['Dados'][0]['2023'])

# Load dataset with short-term rental density (units/km²) by parish for 2021
short_term_rental_density_raw = pd.read_json(r'dados\densidadealojamentosm2.json')
short_term_rental_density = pd.DataFrame(short_term_rental_density_raw['Dados'][0]['2021'])

# Load reference table with official administrative boundaries (CAOP)
municipalities = pd.read_excel(r'dados\Areas_Freg_Conc_Dist_Pais_CAOP2019.xls',
                               sheet_name='Areas_Concelhos_CAOP2019')

All datasets are now successfully loaded into memory and stored in well-labeled variables.
In the next section, we will perform data profiling and initial integration in order to understand their structure and prepare for cleaning and transformation.

2. 🔍 Data Profiling¶

Understanding the structure, completeness, and consistency of the initial datasets is a fundamental step before any integration or analysis can take place. This profiling exercise helped us detect formatting faults, missing values, outliers, and heterogeneity in spatial references.

2.1 Profiling Strategy¶

An explicit profiling function was used to print out the most relevant features of each dataset, including:

  • Data type
  • Missing values (absolute and percentage)
  • Column cardinality (number of unique values)
  • A sample value for each column
In [53]:
def data_profiling(df: pd.DataFrame):
    profiling = pd.DataFrame({
        "Column": df.columns,
        "Type": df.dtypes.values,
        "Nulls (%)": (df.isnull().mean() * 100).round(1),
        "Uniques": df.nunique().values,
        "Example": [df[col].dropna().iloc[0] if df[col].dropna().shape[0] > 0 else None for col in df.columns]
    })

    display(profiling.sort_values("Nulls (%)", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True))

Price Range Distribution¶

To better understand the distribution of property prices, we grouped all listings into manually defined price ranges.

The chart below shows the number of listings in each range, highlighting the concentration around €100K–300K, and confirming the presence of a long tail with high-value properties.

In [58]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns

# Definir bins e labels (não alterar o dataframe original)
price_bins = [0, 50_000, 100_000, 150_000, 200_000, 300_000, 400_000, 500_000, 750_000, 1_000_000, 2_000_000, np.inf]
labels = [
    "≤50K", "50K–100K", "100K–150K", "150K–200K", "200K–300K",
    "300K–400K", "400K–500K", "500K–750K", "750K–1M", "1M–2M", ">2M"
]

prices = pd.to_numeric(property_listings["Price"], errors="coerce")

# Criar coluna temporária com faixas
price_range_temp = pd.cut(prices, bins=price_bins, labels=labels)

# Contagem por faixa
price_range_counts = price_range_temp.value_counts().reindex(labels)

# Gráfico de barras
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
ax = price_range_counts.plot(kind="bar", color="skyblue", edgecolor="black")
plt.title("Distribution of Property Listings by Price Range")
plt.xlabel("Price Range (€)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Listings")
plt.grid(axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)

# Adicionar os valores acima de cada barra
for i, v in enumerate(price_range_counts):
    plt.text(i, v + 50, str(v), ha='center', fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Filtrar preços plausíveis (ex: habitações realistas entre 10K e 750K)
prices = prices[
    (property_listings["Price"] >= 10_000) &
    (property_listings["Price"] <= 750_000)
].copy()

# Boxplot atualizado
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 2.5))
sns.boxplot(x=prices, color="skyblue")
plt.title("Boxplot of Filtered Property Prices")
plt.xlabel("Price (€)")
plt.grid(axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Estatísticas
print("📊 Count:", prices.count())
print("📊 min:", round(prices.min(), 2))
print("📊 25%:", round(prices.quantile(0.25), 2))
print("📊 Mean:", round(prices.mean(), 2))
print("📉 Std Dev:", round(prices.std(), 2))
print("📈 75%:", round(prices.quantile(0.75), 2))
print("📌 Max:", round(prices.max(), 2))

  • The interquartile range (IQR) is between €80,000 and €330,000, and the average price is approximately €229,000.

2.3 Spatial Key Summary¶

Dataset Key Used Notes
municipalities DICO Primary join key (municipality level)
population_density geocod[-4:] Extracted from parish identifier
rental_prices geocod[-4:] Parish to municipality mapping
short_term_rental_density geocod[:4] Parish to municipality mapping
property_listings City, normalized Fuzzy matched to municipality names

Note: The geocod field encodes geographic hierarchy:

  • In parish-level datasets (like short_term_rental_density), the first 4 digits of geocod identify the municipality.
  • In municipality-level datasets (like population_density), the last 4 digits of geocod represent the municipality code directly.

Example:

  • geocod = "150819" in a parish-level dataset → geocod[:4] = "1508" (MunicipalityCode)
  • geocod = "171508" in a municipality-level dataset → geocod[-4:] = "1508" (MunicipalityCode)

This adjustment ensures all datasets can be joined consistently on the same spatial level.

2.4 Cleaning & Normalization Strategy¶

  • Text fields were standardized using lowercase, unidecode, and trimming.
  • Missing values were imputed where regional averages were reliable.
  • Numeric columns were coerced to float and inspected for outliers.
  • Price-based outliers (e.g., listings > €1M or < €10K) were excluded.

2.5 Granularity Adjustment (REVER)¶

To prepare for schema integration, it is necessary that all datasets share the same level of spatial granularity.

  • Parish-level datasets: short_term_rental_density, rental_prices
  • Municipality-level datasets: municipalities, population_density, property_listings

The approach to unify them includes:

  • Extracting the MunicipalityCode key consistently from the geocod field:

    • For parish-level datasets, extract the first 4 digits of geocod (e.g., 150819 → 1508).
    • For municipality-level datasets, extract the last 4 digits of geocod (e.g., 171508 → 1508).

  • Aggregating parish-level data to municipality level by computing the mean per MunicipalityCode, to align with the granularity of municipality-level datasets.

This harmonization ensures that all datasets can be merged and analyzed together reliably.

2.6 Summary of Findings¶

  • 📌 Textual inconsistencies required thorough normalization.
  • 📉 Outliers were identified and filtered.
  • 📎 Key harmonization via MunicipalityCode ensured proper integration.
  • ⚙️ These steps produced a clean, join-ready dataset (dfFinal) suitable for analysis.

3. 🧹 Data Cleaning¶

In this section, we apply all the cleaning and normalization operations identified during the profiling phase.

This includes:

  • Type conversion of indicator columns (valor)
  • Removal of invalid or null entries
  • Standardization of text fields (municipality, region, district)
  • Extraction of MunicipalityCode from geocod
  • Aggregation of parish-level data to municipality level
  • Removal of unwanted columns

3.1 Remove Unwanted Columns¶

During the data cleaning phase, it is essential to remove columns that do not contribute meaningful information, contain mostly missing or irrelevant data, or are outside the project’s scope. This step helps simplify the dataset, reduce noise, and improve the efficiency of subsequent processing and analysis.

Removal Strategy (REVER)¶

  • Property Listings:
    Remove placeholder columns such as those starting with Unnamed: and the Town column, since the project focuses on municipality-level data, not parish-level.

  • Rental Prices and Short-Term Rental Density:
    Drop columns like ind_string, sinal_conv, and sinal_conv_desc as they are duplicates or metadata not useful for analysis.

  • Population Density:
    Remove ind_string, which duplicates information in the valor column.

  • Municipalities:
    Remove geographic or physical measurement columns such as area, perimeter, and altitude which are outside the scope of this project’s analytical objectives.

3.4 Normalize Text Columns¶

The following fields will be normalized:

  • Municipality, District, Region

Normalization steps:

  • Remove accents
  • Convert to lowercase
  • Trim whitespace
  • Store results in new columns ending with _norm

from unidecode import unidecode

def normalize_text(text):
    if pd.isnull(text):
        return ""
    return unidecode(str(text)).lower().strip()

3.4.1 Text Normalization: Municipalities Dataset¶

To ensure robust integration and reliable record linkage, we normalize all relevant textual columns in the municipalities dataset. This includes converting text to lowercase, removing diacritics, and trimming whitespace. The normalized columns will be used throughout the data integration pipeline.

3.5 Extract and Unify MunicipalityCode¶

To enable ongoing merging and aggregation across all datasets, we need to supply each table with a shared identifier for every municipality. It creates a common key, MunicipalityCode, upon which all the data sources are joinable on the municipality level regardless of their initial granularity or format.

Extraction rules applied:

  • For parish-level datasets:
    • short_term_rental_density: first 4 digits of geocod
    • rental_prices: last 4 digits of geocod (INE standard)
  • For municipality-level data (e.g., population_density, municipalities): the MunicipalityCode is obtained as the last 4 digits of the geocod column (or the unique identifier in the reference table).

This process of harmonization is crucial for correct integration, ensuring that all the datasets apply the same standard code in referencing municipalities.

Validation:
We display a sample of each dataset after extracting the MunicipalityCode, confirming the transformation and checking the format of the resulting column.

This unified code will be the main key for all future joins and aggregations. It ensures that each municipality is uniquely and consistently identified, regardless of the dataset's original format or administrative level.

In [76]:
rental_prices["MunicipalityCode"] = rental_prices["geocod"].astype(str).str[-4:]
population_density["MunicipalityCode"] = population_density["geocod"].astype(str).str[-4:]
short_term_rental_density["MunicipalityCode"] = short_term_rental_density["geocod"].astype(str).str[:4:]
municipalities["MunicipalityCode"] = municipalities["DICO"].astype(str).str.zfill(4)

3.6 Aggregating Parish-Level Data to Municipality Level (REVER)¶

Both rental_prices and short_term_rental_density datasets are originally reported at the parish level (freguesia). However, for consistency across all datasets, we need to take these indicators to the municipality level (concelho).

Aggregation Method¶

  • Objective: For every municipality (MunicipalityCode), compute the average value of:
  • Average rent price per square meter (avg_rent_m2)
  • Density of short-term rental units (avg_str_density)
  • Method: Group all records by MunicipalityCode and calculate the average of the indicator values.
  • Handling Missing Data: Following aggregation, there might still be some municipalities without average rent data (because of missing or incomplete data at parish level). To handle this:
  • Missing values are filled with the average rent for the respective district (district_norm). - This guarantees that no municipality will be without an estimated average rent, providing a spatially coherent imputation.
In [77]:
# Convert values to numeric (force "-" and other invalids to NaN)
rental_prices["valor"] = pd.to_numeric(rental_prices["valor"], errors="coerce")
short_term_rental_density["valor"] = pd.to_numeric(short_term_rental_density["valor"], errors="coerce")

# Aggregate mean values by MunicipalityCode
rental_prices_avg = rental_prices.groupby("MunicipalityCode", as_index=False)["valor"].mean().rename(columns={"valor": "avg_rent_m2"})
short_term_rental_density_avg = short_term_rental_density.groupby("MunicipalityCode", as_index=False)["valor"].mean().rename(columns={"valor": "avg_str_density"})

# Merge with municipalities to access district_norm for imputation
rental_prices_avg = rental_prices_avg.merge(
    municipalities[["MunicipalityCode", "district_norm", "region_norm"]],
    on="MunicipalityCode", how="left"
)

# Impute missing avg_rent_m2 with district average
district_means = rental_prices_avg.groupby("district_norm")["avg_rent_m2"].transform("mean")
rental_prices_avg["avg_rent_m2"] = rental_prices_avg["avg_rent_m2"].fillna(district_means)

# Display samples
print("🏠 Sample: Average rent per municipality")
display(rental_prices_avg.head())

print("🏡 Sample: STR density per municipality")
display(short_term_rental_density_avg.head())

3.7 Special Cases Handling¶

During data profiling and identity resolution, a few special cases were detected that require special attention to ensure data quality and correct matching.

3.7.1 Handle Invalid Locations and Ambigous City Names¶

🔍 Issues Detected:¶

  • Duplicate or ambiguous city names:
    For example:

    • "Lagoa (Algarve)" and "Lagoa (São Miguel)" refer to different municipalities but share the same base name "Lagoa".
    • Without disambiguation, fuzzy matching may incorrectly assign listings to the wrong municipality.

  • Invalid or irrelevant locations:

    • "Brasil" appears as a City in some records but is not a Portuguese municipality.
    • "Z - Fora de Portugal" appears in the District field and should be excluded.
✅ Resolution Strategy:¶
  1. Remove invalid locations from the dataset:
    • Filter out listings where the District is "Z - Fora de Portugal" or the City is "Brasil".
In [78]:
# Remove entries clearly outside the target domain
invalid_cities = ["brasil"]
invalid_districts = ["Z - Fora de Portugal"]

property_listings = property_listings[
    (~property_listings["municipality_norm"].isin(invalid_cities)) &
    (~property_listings["District"].isin(invalid_districts))
].copy()
  1. Strip parentheses for fuzzy matching only:
    • Remove parentheses from municipality_norm of listings.
In [79]:
import re

# Função para remover conteúdo entre parênteses
def strip_parentheses(text):
    return re.sub(r"\s*\(.*?\)", "", text).strip()

# Aplicar apenas onde existe parênteses
mask_has_parentheses = property_listings["municipality_norm"].str.contains(r"\(.*\)", regex=True, na=False)
property_listings.loc[mask_has_parentheses, "municipality_norm"] = property_listings.loc[mask_has_parentheses, "municipality_norm"].apply(strip_parentheses)
  1. Create contextual identifiers for identity resolution:
    • Instead of comparing just normalized city names (municipality_norm), we use a new field:
      location_context = municipality_norm + " " + district_norm
    • This provides additional disambiguation when comparing listings to official municipality records.
In [80]:
# create location context string
property_listings["location_context"] = property_listings["municipality_norm"] + " " + property_listings["district_norm"]
municipalities["location_context"] = municipalities["municipality_norm"] + " " + municipalities["district_norm"]

These steps ensure that each listing is assigned the correct MunicipalityCode, improving the quality of downstream analysis and aggregation.

3.7.2 Special Filling for Autonomous Regions (Madeira and Azores) (REVER TEXTO E FORMATAÇÃO)¶

Some municipalities in the Autonomous Regions of Madeira and Azores have missing values for the average rent per square meter (avg_rent_m2).
This is usually due to the lack of source data for some or all parishes in these regions.

To ensure a consistent and complete dataset for all municipalities, we apply a stepwise imputation:

1. District-Level Imputation¶

For most mainland municipalities, missing avg_rent_m2 values are filled with the average rent for their respective district (district_norm), as performed in 3.6 Aggregating Parish-Level Data to Municipality Level

# Already performed above:
district_means = rental_prices_avg.groupby("district_norm")["avg_rent_m2"].transform("mean")
rental_prices_avg["avg_rent_m2"] = rental_prices_avg["avg_rent_m2"].fillna(district_means)

2. Regional Imputation for Madeira and Azores¶

For municipalities in Madeira and Azores where the district-level imputation still results in missing values (due to the absence of data in their entire district), we use the regional average as a fallback.

  • The average rent per square meter is calculated across all municipalities in the respective region (Madeira or Azores).

  • Only municipalities with missing values and belonging to "madeira" or "acores" in the region_norm field are filled this way.

In [81]:
# Calculate region-level means
madeira_region_avg = rental_prices_avg[
    rental_prices_avg["region_norm"].str.contains("madeira", case=False, na=False)
]["avg_rent_m2"].mean()

azores_region_avg = rental_prices_avg[
    rental_prices_avg["region_norm"].str.contains("acores", case=False, na=False)
]["avg_rent_m2"].mean()

# Apply regional imputation for Madeira and Azores
def fill_missing_rent(row):
    if pd.isna(row["avg_rent_m2"]):
        if "madeira" in str(row["region_norm"]).lower():
            return madeira_region_avg
        elif "acores" in str(row["region_norm"]).lower():
            return azores_region_avg
    return row["avg_rent_m2"]

rental_prices_avg["avg_rent_m2"] = rental_prices_avg.apply(fill_missing_rent, axis=1)
⚠️ Impact of the Imputation Decision¶

Filling missing average rent values using regional averages involves a trade-off between data completeness and local specificity:

  • Loss of local variation: Replacing missing values with regional averages smooths out differences that may exist within the municipalities themselves, reducing data granularity.

  • Improved spatial completeness: This imputation avoids excluding entire municipalities from the analysis, which could bias the results or reduce the study’s coverage.

  • Adequacy for project scope: Considering the objective of regional analysis and the limited data availability in autonomous regions, this approach is appropriate and maintains overall dataset coherence.

  • Transparency: It is essential to explicitly mention this decision in the study limitations and consider it when interpreting results, especially in analyses involving regional rent comparisons.

This compromise allows maximizing the use of available data, balancing statistical rigor and contextual knowledge.

4. Data Integration & Identity Resolution (REVER)¶

Since the property_listings dataset lacks geographic codes (MunicipalityCode), we must match listings to municipalities based on the normalized municipality name (municipality_norm).

We use a fuzzy matching approach with three components:

  1. Blocking: Limit comparisons to likely candidates using the first 4 characters of normalized names;
  2. Similarity Scoring: Use 3 complementary metrics from the RapidFuzz library:
    • token_sort_ratio: handles reordering of words;
    • token_set_ratio: handles subsets and partial overlaps;
    • ratio: computes raw character-level similarity (Levenshtein);
  3. Thresholding: Only matches the pair with the highest Similiarity Score to ensure reliability.

This step allows us to associate listings with a MunicipalityCode, enabling integration with other datasets.

In [82]:
# Create blocking key from normalized names
property_listings['block_key'] = property_listings['location_context'].str[:4]
municipalities['block_key'] = municipalities['location_context'].str[:4]

4.1 Candidate Pair Generation¶

To further reduce computational cost and avoid unnecessary comparisons, we generate candidate pairs by joining both datasets (property_listings and municipalities) on the block_key field. The block_key is derived from the first 4 characters of the normalized location_context (which combines normalized municipality and district names).

This step ensures that only records with similar prefixes are compared in the subsequent fuzzy matching step, greatly improving efficiency.

At this stage, we are only generating candidate pairs — the final match decision will be based on similarity scores computed in the next step.

In [83]:

    property_listings[['City', 'municipality_norm', 'district_norm', 'location_context', 'block_key']],
    municipalities[['MunicipalityCode', 'municipality_norm', 'district_norm', 'location_context', 'block_key']],
    on='block_key',
    suffixes=('_listings', '_municipality')
)

4.2 Calculation of Similarity Score (FALTA FALAR DO SIM_RATIO)¶

For each pair generated in the final stage, we compute text similarity scores to measure the similarity of each listing to each municipality. We use a combination of three different metrics from the RapidFuzz library:

  • token_sort_ratio: Doesn't care about word order; useful for comparing names such as "vila real" and "real vila".
  • token_set_ratio: Handles subset matching and duplicate words; good for partial matching. - ratio: Character-level raw Levenshtein similarity; small typos and minor differences are indicated.

All measures of similarity are scaled to the range 0 to 1, with 1 being a perfect similarity.

The final similarity_score is then the mean of the three measures and is a comprehensive assessment of the string similarity.

In [84]:
from rapidfuzz import fuzz

# Step 3: Compute similarity scores
candidates['sim_token_sort'] = candidates.apply(
    lambda row: fuzz.token_sort_ratio(row['location_context_listings'], row['location_context_municipality']) / 100,
    axis=1
)

candidates['sim_token_set'] = candidates.apply(
    lambda row: fuzz.token_set_ratio(row['location_context_listings'], row['location_context_municipality']) / 100,
    axis=1
)

candidates['sim_ratio'] = candidates.apply(
    lambda row: fuzz.ratio(row['location_context_listings'], row['location_context_municipality']) / 100,
    axis=1
)
In [85]:
candidates["similarity_score"] = np.mean(
    candidates[["sim_token_sort", "sim_token_set", "sim_ratio"]], axis=1
)

4.3 Filtering the Best Matches¶

To achieve high-confidence matching, we narrow down the candidate pairs to retain the highest similarity_score pair per city. similarity_score is the mean value of the three measurements (sim_token_sort, sim_token_set, and sim_ratio).

If a listing can belong to more than one municipality, we use the highest score in this case. This enables us to achieve one-to-one mapping between each listing and a municipality with no duplicate or ambiguous assignments allowed.

Why choose the pair with the highest similarity score?

We will assign a distinct unique MunicipalityCode to each listing, so each such listing will be in the dataset and will not get duplicated. With the highest similarity score, we are maximizing the probability of obtaining a correct matching based on all available evidence of string similarity. This approach also facilitates easy resolution of identity and is simple to audit and computationally straightforward.

In [86]:

4.4 Assign Municipality Code to Listings¶

After determining the best match for each listing, we assign the corresponding MunicipalityCode to every property listing.
This enables aggregation and integration of the listings data with all other datasets at the municipality level.

The merge is performed using the location_context string, ensuring each property is linked to the correct municipality.

In [87]:
# Assign MunicipalityCode to each listing by merging with the matches DataFrame
property_listings_matched = property_listings.merge(
    matches[['location_context_listings', 'MunicipalityCode']],
    left_on='location_context',
    right_on='location_context_listings',
    how='left'
).drop(columns=['location_context_listings'])

4.5 Municipality Aggregation of Listings (REVER CODIGO E CRIAR SECCAO PARA O MERGE PARA DFFINAL SEPARADO)¶

Now that each property listing is associated with a MunicipalityCode, we can aggregate statistics at the municipal level.

For every municipality, we calculate:

  • avg_price: Average price of property sold.
  • count_listings: A count of the number of listings in that municipality.

Having calculated these aggregates, we join them with the primary key table of municipalities, and also:

  • Average rent per square meter (avg_rent_m2) - Average short-term rental density (avg_str_density)
  • Population density (population_density) The final combined dataset, dfFinal, combines all the pertinent indicators at the municipal level, and is utilized for all subsequent analytics and visualizations.

The resulting integrated dataset, dfFinal, brings together all relevant indicators at the municipality level, and is used for all downstream analytics and visualizations.

).reset_index()

5. Data Warehouse and Data Marts (REVER O QUE ESTA AQUI ESCRITO E VER SE NÃO FALTA MAIS NADA (SERÁ ISTO MAIS PARA O RELATORIO? FAZ SENTIDO FALAR DISTO?)¶

For this project, we constructed a centralized data warehouse that integrates all relevant datasets into a unified schema based on the municipality level (MunicipalityCode). This integrated dataset consolidates information on property listings, rental prices, population density, and short-term rental density, enabling comprehensive analysis of the housing market dynamics in Portugal.

Data Marts Description¶

From the data warehouse, we derived specialized data marts that support specific analytical queries:

  • Property Market Mart: Contains aggregated data on average property sale prices and counts of listings per municipality.
  • Rental Market Mart: Includes average rental prices per square meter by municipality.
  • Demographic Mart: Houses population density and other demographic indicators.
  • Short-Term Rentals Mart: Provides density of short-term rental units by municipality.

These data marts enable focused analysis on:

  • Relationships between housing prices and rental markets.
  • Correlations between demographic density and housing supply.
  • Impact assessments of short-term rentals on rental prices and housing availability.

Limitations and Extensions¶

  • Some municipalities lack listings data due to data unavailability, limiting the scope of certain analyses.
  • Future work could extend the data warehouse with additional sources such as income levels, urban mobility, or economic indicators to enrich the analysis.
  • Data marts are constructed from aggregated data, which may mask intra-municipality variations.

This structured approach facilitates modular, scalable analytics and supports answering both current and future research questions.

In this notebook, both the data warehouse and data marts are implemented as Pandas DataFrames, allowing for flexible analytical queries and rapid prototyping. No external database systems were used in this phase.

6. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) (TROCAR VISUALIZATIONS COM EDA DE SITIO? REVER E REPENSAR GRAFICOS)¶

6.1 Overview and Data Distribution¶

In this section, we analyze the distribution of the key project variables: average sale price, average rent price per m², population density, and short-term rental density. Understanding the spread, central tendency, and presence of outliers will help guide subsequent analyses and provide initial insights into the structure of the housing market across Portuguese municipalities.

For each variable, we present:

  • Histogram (with optional kernel density estimate)
  • Boxplot (to visualize spread and outliers)
  • Descriptive statistics (mean, std, quartiles, etc.)

We also compute correlation coefficients (Pearson and Spearman) between these variables to understand both linear and monotonic relationships. The variables analyzed are:

  • Average Property Sale Price (avg_price)
  • Average Rent Price per m² (avg_rent_m2)
  • Population Density (population_density)
  • Short-Term Rental Density (avg_str_density)

These analyses help to detect trends, outliers, and potential relationships, providing a strong foundation for more advanced statistical modeling.

6.2 Correlation Matrix and Significance¶

To further explore relationships among the key variables, we compute both Pearson and Spearman correlation matrices. These show how strongly each variable is associated with the others, using both linear (Pearson) and rank-based (Spearman) correlation.

We also compute p-values for the Pearson correlations to assess statistical significance. P-values below 0.05 indicate a statistically significant correlation.

This analysis helps us understand whether, for example, higher short-term rental density is associated with higher prices or population density.

In [92]:
import scipy.stats as stats
import pandas as pd

eda_df = dfFinal[variables].dropna()

pearson_corr = eda_df.corr(method="pearson")
spearman_corr = eda_df.corr(method="spearman")

print("Pearson Correlation Matrix:")
display(pearson_corr)

print("Spearman Correlation Matrix:")
display(spearman_corr)

def correlation_pvalues(df):
    dfcols = pd.DataFrame(columns=df.columns)
    pvals = dfcols.transpose().join(dfcols, how='outer')
    for r in df.columns:
        for c in df.columns:
            if r == c:
                pvals[r][c] = 0.0
            else:
                _, pval = stats.pearsonr(df[r], df[c])
                pvals[r][c] = round(pval, 4)
    return pvals

print("Pearson Correlation p-values:")
display(correlation_pvalues(eda_df))

6.3 Bivariate Relationships and Scatterplots¶

Understanding how variables relate to each other visually can reveal trends, clusters, or outliers not apparent in summary statistics.

We explore:

  • The relationship between average sale price and average rent
  • The association between population density and both price variables
  • The relationship between short-term rental density and the other variables

Scatterplots help assess linearity, potential non-linear trends, and identify potential clusters or outliers.

6.3.1 Scatterplots for Key Pairs¶

We use scatterplots to visualize each pair of main variables.

In [93]:
pairs = [
    ("avg_price", "avg_rent_m2"),
    ("population_density", "avg_str_density"),
    ("population_density", "avg_rent_m2"),
    ("population_density", "avg_price")
]

for x_var, y_var in pairs:
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    sns.regplot(data=dfFinal, x=x_var, y=y_var, scatter_kws={"alpha":0.6}, line_kws={"color":"red"})
    plt.title(f"{x_var.replace('_', ' ').title()} vs {y_var.replace('_', ' ').title()}")
    plt.xlabel(x_var.replace('_', ' ').title())
    plt.ylabel(y_var.replace('_', ' ').title())
    plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

6.3.2 Key Insights from Scatterplots¶

  • Avg Sale Price vs Avg Rent per m²:
    There is a positive trend between the average property sale price and the average rent per m². Municipalities with higher sale prices tend to also have higher rental prices, but the spread is considerable, indicating other factors at play.

  • Population Density vs Short-Term Rental Density:
    A strong positive linear relationship is evident. Denser municipalities almost always have higher short-term rental densities, reflecting urban tourism pressure.

  • Population Density vs Avg Rent per m²:
    There is a positive association, but with significant variance. Densely populated areas tend to have higher rents, yet there are exceptions (possibly due to regional or local market dynamics).

  • Population Density vs Avg Sale Price:
    There is a positive linear trend: more densely populated municipalities generally exhibit higher average sale prices, but outliers and spread suggest that other factors (e.g., local amenities, tourism, or economic activity) play a significant role.

Overall:

  • The relationships are generally positive, but not all are equally strong.
  • The tightest relationship is observed between population density and STR density.
  • Both rent and sale prices increase with density, but with considerable heterogeneity—suggesting multiple market drivers.

6.4 Group Comparisons (Metro vs Non-Metro)¶

We compare the distributions of key indicators between metropolitan municipalities (Lisbon and Porto metro areas) and non-metropolitan ones using boxplots.

First, we retrieve the municipality codes of Lisbon and Porto metro areas from our dataset to define the groups accurately.

In [94]:
# Identify Lisbon and Porto metropolitan municipalities using the normalized region names
lisbon_municipalities = dfFinal.loc[dfFinal["region_norm"] == "area metropolitana de lisboa", "municipality_norm"].tolist()
porto_municipalities = dfFinal.loc[dfFinal["region_norm"] == "area metropolitana do porto", "municipality_norm"].tolist()

lisbon_metro_codes = dfFinal[dfFinal["municipality_norm"].isin(lisbon_municipalities)]["MunicipalityCode"].tolist()
porto_metro_codes = dfFinal[dfFinal["municipality_norm"].isin(porto_municipalities)]["MunicipalityCode"].tolist()

# Flag municipalities as metropolitan or not
dfFinal['is_metro'] = dfFinal['MunicipalityCode'].isin(lisbon_metro_codes + porto_metro_codes)

indicators = ["avg_price", "avg_rent_m2", "population_density"]

for var in indicators:
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    sns.boxplot(x='is_metro', y=var, data=dfFinal)
    plt.title(f"{var.replace('_', ' ').title()}: Metro vs Non-Metro")
    plt.xlabel("Is Metro Area")
    plt.ylabel(var.replace('_', ' ').title())
    plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Analysis of Results¶

  • Average Price: Metro areas show higher average sale prices than non-metro areas. The spread is smaller, but the central value (median) is clearly higher for metro municipalities.
  • Average Rent Price: Metro municipalities have higher rent prices per m², confirming the expected urban premium.
  • Population Density: As expected, metro municipalities have much higher population densities. There are also more outliers in non-metro areas, possibly due to some small municipalities with high local density (e.g., tourist zones).

Insights:

  • There is a significant urban premium in both property sale and rental markets.
  • Metro areas are much denser and more expensive, both to buy and to rent.
  • This separation justifies analyzing metro and non-metro markets separately for more targeted policy and investment recommendations.

6.5 Simple Linear Regression Analysis¶

To further investigate the relationships between key variables, we fit simple linear regression models. These models help quantify how much variables such as population density or average rent explain variation in average property sale price at the municipality level.

We report model coefficients, R² values, and discuss the practical significance of the results.

In [95]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

# Prepare data for regression
reg_df = dfFinal[["avg_price", "population_density", "avg_rent_m2"]].dropna()

# Model 1: Predict avg_price from population_density
X1 = sm.add_constant(reg_df["population_density"])
model1 = sm.OLS(reg_df["avg_price"], X1).fit()
print(model1.summary())

# Model 2: Predict avg_price from avg_rent_m2
X2 = sm.add_constant(reg_df["avg_rent_m2"])
model2 = sm.OLS(reg_df["avg_price"], X2).fit()
print(model2.summary())

Interpretation of Regression Results¶

  • Model 1 (Population Density):
    The regression coefficient for population density is 32.84, meaning that for every additional inhabitant per km², the average sale price increases by about €33, on average, ceteris paribus.
    The R² of 0.139 suggests that population density explains ~14% of the variance in average property prices across municipalities.
    The relationship is statistically significant (p < 0.001), but most of the price variability remains unexplained by this single factor.

  • Model 2 (Average Rent Price per m²):
    The coefficient for average rent is 11,010, meaning that a €1 increase in average rent per m² is associated with an increase of about €11,000 in average property sale price.
    The R² of 0.104 means that average rent explains about 10% of the variance in sale prices.
    Again, the relationship is significant (p < 0.001), but other unobserved variables play a major role.

Limitations:
Both models have low explanatory power (low R²), indicating that other factors—such as local amenities, income, or urban infrastructure—may strongly affect property prices. Results suggest moderate but meaningful associations between density/rent and sale price.

Conclusion:
While both population density and average rent are significant predictors of property values at the municipality level, they individually explain only a modest proportion of the variation. This highlights the complexity of the housing market and the need for richer datasets and models in future work.

Why This EDA? Rationale and Interpretation (REVER FAZ SENTIDO FALAR DISTO?)¶

The exploratory data analysis (EDA) in this notebook was designed to answer the following research questions:

  • How do key variables (sale price, rent, population density, STR density) distribute across Portuguese municipalities?
  • What relationships exist between these variables?
  • Do metropolitan municipalities (Lisbon and Porto) differ significantly from others?
  • Can simple regression models quantify the effect of population density and rent on sale price?

Why use these metrics and visualizations?¶

  1. Histograms and Boxplots:
    Used to understand the distribution (center, spread, outliers) of each variable. This helps identify whether some municipalities are atypical or if values are concentrated in certain ranges.

  2. Correlation Matrices (Pearson & Spearman):

    • Pearson correlation detects linear associations between variables (e.g., does higher density linearly predict higher prices?).
    • Spearman correlation checks monotonic relationships (important if variables don’t relate linearly, but higher values still tend to follow higher/lower values).
    • These analyses answer: Are the variables associated? How strongly?

  3. Scatterplots with Regression Lines:

    • Visualize whether observed correlations are driven by a handful of points (outliers) or show a general trend.
    • Regression lines provide a sense of linearity and allow quick visual assessment of trend direction.

  4. Group Comparisons (Metro vs Non-Metro):

    • Directly test if "context" (being in a metro area or not) translates to differences in prices, rent, or density.
    • Boxplots visually summarize differences in distributions.

  5. Simple Linear Regression:

    • Quantifies the expected change in sale price for each unit change in population density or rent.
    • R² statistic measures how much of the price variation is explained by each variable.

Why these particular variables?¶

  • All chosen variables are available across municipalities, interpretable, and reflect factors discussed in the literature on urban housing markets.
  • Sale price and rent: Direct economic signals.
  • Population density and STR density: Capture both demographic pressure and tourism/short-term rental market influence.

Which Questions Are Answered?¶

  • What is the typical range and spread of each key variable?
    (→ See descriptive stats, histograms, boxplots)

  • Are variables related, and how strongly?
    (→ Correlation matrices and scatterplots show the strength and direction)

  • Are metro areas systematically different?
    (→ Boxplots by metro status)

  • Can population density or rent explain property prices?
    (→ Regression models quantify the relationships)

Limitations¶

  • Unexplained variation:
    Low R² in regressions means that many important factors are not captured.
  • Causality:
    Correlation and regression do not imply causation—findings show association, not cause-effect.
  • Granularity:
    Municipality-level aggregation may hide important intra-city patterns.

Summary¶

The EDA provides a quantitative and visual foundation for understanding the dynamics of the Portuguese housing market. It answers the main research questions but also highlights the need for richer, more granular data and more complex models in future analyses.

7. Spatial Visualizations: Geographic Patterns (SERÁ QUE ESTES MAPAS COM VARIAVEIS SIMPLES TRAZEM MUITOS INSIGHTS? ADICIONAR O TAL DE RATIO AVG_PRICE/LISTINGS OU OUTROS?)¶

After exploring the statistical distribution and relationships between the main variables, we now turn to their spatial patterns across Portuguese municipalities.
Choropleth maps are used to visualize how short-term rental density, property prices, and rent levels are distributed geographically.

7.1 Geospatial Preparation¶

To allow for spatial visualization, we combine multiple regional GeoJSON files (Continente, Madeira, Açores) in a single one. This needs to be executed once and is used as a background layer for any subsequent visualizations.

What is a GeoJSON?¶

A GeoJSON is a standard file format to represent geographic features as JSON. It stores both the geometry (shapes, such as boundaries) and attributes (such as municipality name or code) of a feature. Each entry typically represents an area (such as a municipality) with a polygon defining its limits.

What was made¶

  • We downloaded 5 separate GeoJSON files covering:
  • Mainland Portugal
  • Madeira
  • Azores (3 sub-regions)
  • These files were derived from the open-source repository: https://github.com/nmota/caop_GeoJSON
  • Each file contained slight schema differences (e.g., column names), so we:
    • Standardized column names like DICO, Concelho, and NUTS levels
    • Projected all geometries to the WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) coordinate reference system
  • Merged them into one single GeoJSON file: Portugal_Municipalities.geojson
  • Smushed geometries to accelerate map rendering
  • Made a temporary change to dfFinal, to replace NaN with 0, to enable municipalities with no values in avg_price and count_listings to still be rendered in section 7.2.
  • It is now used in all ensuing section 7.1 onwards visualizations.

Only has to be done once, and resulting GeoJSON is used as a base map, and not an analytical dataset.

# Load and merge regional GeoJSONs
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import json
import plotly.express as px

geojson_paths = [
    "dados/geojsons/ContinenteConcelhos.geojson",
    "dados/geojsons/MadeiraConcelhos.geojson",
    "dados/geojsons/AçoresOcidentalConcelhos.geojson",
    "dados/geojsons/AçoresOrientalConcelhos.geojson",
    "dados/geojsons/AçoresCentralConcelhos.geojson"
]

def normalize_schema(gdf):
    rename_map = {
        "Dico": "DICO",
        "Municipio": "Concelho",
        "Nut3_dsg": "NUTIII_DSG",
        "Nut2_dsg": "NUTII_DSG",
        "Nut1_dsg": "NUTI_DSG",
        "Ilha": "Distrito"
    }
    gdf = gdf.rename(columns={k: v for k, v in rename_map.items() if k in gdf.columns})
    if "DICO" in gdf.columns:
        gdf["DICO"] = gdf["DICO"].fillna(gdf.get("DICO"))
    return gdf

gdf_list = [normalize_schema(gpd.read_file(p).to_crs(epsg=4326)) for p in geojson_paths]
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pd.concat(gdf_list), crs="EPSG:4326")
gdf["geometry"] = gdf["geometry"].simplify(tolerance=0.005)
gdf.to_file("dados/geojsons/Portugal_Municipalities.geojson", driver="GeoJSON")

dfFinal["avg_price"] = dfFinal["avg_price"].fillna(0)
dfFinal["count_listings"] = dfFinal["count_listings"].fillna(0)

7.2 STR Density per Municipality¶

The following interactive map shows the density of short-term rental (STR) units per municipality. This measure represents the tourism accommodation intensity relative to the municipality size, in units per km².

STR density is typically associated with:

  • Urbanizations and historic city centers;
  • Coastal tourist zones;
  • Islands such as Madeira and Azores.

The interactive map allows:

  • STR "hotspots" identification
  • How STR presence varies over territory.

7.3 Municipality Average Property Price¶

This map displays the spatial pattern of average property sale prices between Portuguese municipalities. It provides instant judgment of regional variations in real estate markets and helps in the identification of high-value "hotspots", specifically in:

  • Metropolitan cities such as Lisbon and Porto
  • Touristic coastlines such as Cascais, Loulé, and Albufeira
  • Autonomous territories, such as Funchal in Madeira

These trends in price are not only reflective of local demand and supply forces, but also of the influence of external factors including short-term rental use, tourist pressure, and accessibility.

📌 How patterns interrelate with other metrics like rent and STR density will be explored in the next sections. (REVER)

7.4 Average Long-Term Rental Price per m² by Municipality¶

This is the spatial distribution of average long-term rental prices per square meter across Portuguese municipalities.

Higher rent prices tend to cluster in:

  • Metropolitan areas, especially Lisbon and Porto
  • Tourism areas, such as the Algarve, Madeira, and some parts of the Azores

These regions tend to have increased housing pressure, both internally from local residents' demand and externally from sources such as short-term rentals, second-home buying, and seasonal tourism.

Regions in the interior of the country will generally have lower levels of rent, as would be typical for broader trends of depopulation and decreased demand.

📌 In the EDA, more advanced analysis will explore the relationship of STR density, sale price, and population concentration to rental price.

7.5 Population Density by Municipality¶

This map shows the population density (inhabitants per km²) of every Portuguese municipality. Darker tones represent areas of higher residential concentration, typically urban or peri-urban areas such as Lisbon, Porto, and Funchal.

Main observations:

  • The Lisbon Metropolitan Area stands out clearly, showing intense demographic pressure.
  • Other island municipalities, particularly in Madeira, also have high densities despite smaller land masses.
  • Rural inland areas, such as in Alentejo or Trás-os-Montes, present the lowest population densities.

This geographic context is important to place in context how demand and housing pressure can vary based on where people actually live.

7.6 Municipality Number of Listings¶

This map shows the number of property listings (for sale) per municipality, derived from the merged dataset. It highlights places with high market activity in real estate, likely due to urbanization, tourism, and economic hubs.

Key findings:

  • As would be anticipated, Lisbon, Porto, and Algarve coastal municipalities top the list in number of listings.
  • Some of the proposed small cities are spikes in listings, Stratum maybe due to tourism hotspots or high STR activity.
  • Very few or no listings in a location likely reflect rural locations or unreliability of data.

It serves to¶

quantify market visibility and act as a proxy for housing transaction intensity between places.

Insights (REVER. INSIGHTS GERAIS vs INSIGHTS POR VISUALIZAÇÃO)¶

  • Urban centers (Lisbon, Porto) and coastal tourist destinations stand out with higher STR densities and property prices.
  • Spatial heterogeneity: Not all high-value or high-STR municipalities are in Lisbon/Porto; the Algarve, Madeira, and Azores also show local peaks.
  • Mapping enables quick identification of “pressure zones” where policy intervention may be most urgent.

These spatial visualizations provide actionable insights into the geographic dimension of Portugal’s housing market dynamics, supplementing the EDA with a “where” perspective.

8. 📌 Conclusions (REVER OBVIAMENTE ACABAR A ANALISE PARA PODER TIRAR CONCLUSÕES)¶

This section summarizes the key findings and insights obtained from the data integration and analysis process. It connects the results back to the original research questions and highlights the added value of the integration work.

Main Findings¶

  • There is a clear positive correlation between short-term rental density and both rent and sale prices, especially in urban centers and coastal areas.
  • Metropolitan municipalities (Lisbon, Porto) and tourism-intensive zones show significantly higher STR density and property values.
  • Population density acts as a proxy for housing pressure and aligns spatially with higher market activity.
  • Regression models suggest that while population density and rent prices are statistically significant predictors of sale price, they only explain a small part of the variability — pointing to the complexity of housing market dynamics.

9. 🚧 Limitations¶

While the project successfully integrates multiple heterogeneous data sources and explores the relationship between short-term rentals (STR), rent prices, and housing supply, several limitations must be acknowledged:

1. 📍 Spatial Granularity¶

  • The final integrated dataset operates at the municipality level. This aggregation can mask intra-municipality variation, especially in large urban areas where housing pressure and STR activity are highly localized (e.g., Lisbon historic center vs. outskirts).

2. 🧩 Missing Variables¶

  • The analysis does not include potentially important predictors such as average income, employment rates, urban planning constraints, or transport accessibility, which could further explain variability in rent and sale prices.

3. 🕒 Temporal Limitations¶

  • The data is cross-sectional, with STR data from 2021, and rent/sale/population data from 2023. This mismatch limits causal interpretation and hinders time-series or trend analyses.

4. ⚠️ Imputation Effects¶

  • Incomplete rent data was imputed using district or regional averages (especially for Madeira and Azores). While this preserves spatial coverage, it introduces bias by smoothing over local variation.

5. ✍️ Identity Resolution Errors¶

  • Despite the use of multiple similarity metrics, fuzzy matching may introduce incorrect associations between listings and municipalities, especially when dealing with ambiguous or missing location names.

6. 🏗️ STR Data Limitations¶

  • STR density data is from 2021 and only available at parish level, requiring aggregation and transformation to match other datasets. This may reduce temporal and geographic accuracy, particularly in rapidly changing urban areas.

These limitations should be considered when interpreting the results, and future work should aim to refine spatial precision, expand variable coverage, and explore longitudinal patterns.

10. 🔁 Peer Review Reflections and Phase 1 Improvements¶

This section summarizes how peer feedback and Phase 1 results shaped the final implementation of the project. The improvements span clarity, completeness, and analytical rigor.

🎯 Improvements Based on Peer Review Feedback¶

The project received valuable suggestions during the peer review phase. Below is a summary of the key points raised and how they were addressed:

Feedback Action Taken
The Kaggle dataset was underutilized (only 3 columns used) ✅ Future work now considers incorporating more variables (e.g., area, typology), and this limitation is noted explicitly
Lack of Data Profiling and Cleaning sections ✅ Added comprehensive profiling for each dataset and a detailed cleaning plan
Poor explanation of Entity Resolution ✅ Fully rewritten ER section with explanation of blocking, similarity metrics (3 types), score aggregation, and matching strategy
Redundant columns and lack of schema clarity ✅ Removed unnecessary columns and created a normalized, well-justified integrated schema (dfFinal)
Missing values still present in rent and STR datasets ✅ Imputed missing rent values using district and regional averages (with justification); gaps are acknowledged in Limitations
No discussion of outliers ✅ Outliers identified and discussed through boxplots and descriptive stats, particularly for avg_price and avg_rent_m2
Use of ambiguous term "alojamento" (housing vs STR) ✅ Clarified in Limitations that STR refers specifically to short-term tourist accommodations
More dataset examples should be shown (head(), sample()) ✅ Now included throughout profiling and cleaning steps
Notebook had redundant/repetitive blocks ⚠️ Some repetition remains for clarity, but structure is now clearer and cleaner

🔄 Improvements from Phase 1 to Phase 2¶

Several key improvements were made between project phases, beyond what was addressed through peer review:

Area Phase 1 Phase 2
Data Integration Preliminary merges without full granularity alignment Full harmonization of spatial units at municipality level, with proper aggregation of parish-level data
Identity Resolution Manual or ad-hoc matching Automated fuzzy matching pipeline using RapidFuzz with multiple metrics and thresholding
Imputation Strategy Missing values left untreated District and regional mean imputation applied to ensure complete spatial coverage
Exploratory Analysis Limited to value distributions Added correlation matrices, scatterplots, regression models, metro vs non-metro comparisons
Spatial Visualizations Absent or basic Full set of interactive choropleths showing spatial patterns of STR density, rent, sale price, population, and listings
Reproducibility Basic data cleaning Clear structure, code modularity, reusable functions, and documented transformations

✨ Summary¶

The peer review process significantly improved the clarity, structure, and robustness of the project. Combined with internal review of Phase 1 limitations, these contributions resulted in a more rigorous, complete, and well-documented final analysis.

📌 Remaining limitations and opportunities for improvement are acknowledged in the Limitations and Future Work sections.
